title: The Guarded Threshold: Why the Lineages Watch the Door
dek: Cranes, parrots and lotus vines carved around a hotel entrance. On the toraṇa, and the oldest job in South Asian art.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: An arched walnut doorframe densely carved with cranes, parrots, lotus buds and vines, lit by a warm halo of concealed light, standing in a bare plaster wall with a hotel lobby visible through the open doors.
excerpt: Every wall in this picture is bare except one place. A concept study in the oldest siting decision in South Asian art: ornament belongs at the crossing.

title: Earth as Palette: The Mineral Life of Color
dek: Lapis, ochre, marigold and crushed shell on a grinding slab. On varṇa, and why the oldest palettes still read as luxury.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: Five heaps of raw pigment on a granite grinding slab: lapis blue, red ochre, marigold yellow, raw sienna and crushed shell white, beside a stone muller and a brass bowl holding a brush.
excerpt: Before a lineage has a style, it has a geology. What sits on the grinding slab above is not a color scheme; it is a map of the ground the tradition stands on.

title: The Grammar of the Grid: Proportion as a Sacred Discipline
dek: Before a single figure is drawn, the grid is drawn. On tālamāna, the proportional systems that let sacred art survive translation.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: An iconometry study on cream handmade paper: a seated figure drawn inside a red proportional grid annotated with measurements, with a bamboo ruler, ink pot and brush on the worn table beside it.
excerpt: The drawing above begins not with the figure but with the measured cage around it. A curatorial argument for proportion as the most translatable thing a lineage owns.

title: Romance Meets Materiality: Sentiment, Specification, and the Commissioned Wall
dek: Every commission begins twice: once as longing, and once as a set of documents. The craft is refusing to let either erase the other.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: A pencil-line scroll of peacocks unrolled beside a tube of indigo paint, and at right the finished monochrome panel framed on a white corridor wall above marble floors.
excerpt: One half of this image is a drawing on a table. The other half is an artwork passing plan review. On the two loves inside every commission, and why the atelier refuses to choose between them.

title: Carved by Light: Shadow, Relief, and the South Asian Wall
dek: A relief has no color of its own until light arrives. On shadow as the atelier's other material.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: A monochrome carved peacock relief on a dark plaster wall, its fanned tail modeled by a single wash of light from the cove above.
excerpt: Pigment tells a wall what to say. Light decides whether anyone hears it. A study of the light a carved surface lives under: raking daylight, gallery beams, and the long amber evening.

title: The Architecture of Quiet: Acoustic Craft and the Heritage Surface
dek: Why the oldest instincts of South Asian craft, relief, repetition, and fiber, turn out to be acoustic design by another name.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: A conference room whose full back wall is wrapped in charcoal acoustic felt patterned with the Kūrma motif in copper, behind a long walnut table and a wall display.
excerpt: We remember rooms by how they sound almost as vividly as by how they look. A curatorial argument for treating the acoustic surface as a site of heritage art rather than a technical afterthought.

title: The Translatability of Tradition: Curating South Asian Heritage Lineages for Contemporary Architecture
dek: Which indigenous lineages carry the geometric rigour to leave the page and become permanent built surface, and which remain exploratory.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: Comparative study of South Asian heritage lineages assessed for architectural translatability.
excerpt: Authentic curatorial translation does not simply copy a heritage artform or painting onto a wall; it extracts the underlying geometric tension of the lineage and gives it structural resonance within modern space.

title: The Sūtra & the Senses: A Curatorial Inquiry into Visual Fluency, Ancient Morphology, and Built Space
dek: What visual neuroscience suggests about why ancestral geometries feel restful, and where the honest limits of that argument lie.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: Diagram relating the grammar of ancestral form, symmetry, grouping and fractal dimension, to built architectural surfaces.
excerpt: To examine Indian geometry through a neuroaesthetic lens is not to reduce sacred art to biology, but to explore how ancient visual masters intuitively calibrated form to the structural architecture of human perception.

title: Beyond the Paisley: Ancient Morphology, Architectural Materiality, and the Quiet Luxury of the Bīja
dek: The curved teardrop dismissed as “paisley” was never ornament. It is a germinating seed contour, and it carries architectural weight.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: Diagram titled The Morphology of the Bīja, charting the regional variants of the seed contour across Kashmir, Andhra Pradesh, Bengal, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan and Gujarat.
excerpt: Long before industrial looms flattened its geometry into two-dimensional novelty, the bīja was an architectural prayer, a concentrated nucleus of life holding immense kinetic energy within an asymmetric curve.

title: The Living Axis: Translating Zoomorphic and Botanical Lineages into Contemporary Architecture
dek: Five archetypal geometries, Vṛkṣa, Kūrma, Matsya, Mayūra and Āraṇya, recovered from decorative trivialisation and returned to architectural materiality.
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: Curatorial diagram of the five archetypal South Asian geometries and their translation into architectural relief.
excerpt: In classical South Asian spatial thought, zoomorphic and botanical motifs were never decorative flourishes; they were structural equations balancing cosmic order against built space.

title: From Brushstroke to Bas-Relief
dek: Translating South Asian Heritage Lineages into Restorative Architecture
author: Preeti Padaley
authorBio: Founder & Principal Curator, Artha Indus Atelier. MBBS, MHSA, PMP.
imageAlt: A carved bas-relief medallion in pale plaster, ringed with Warli figures and wave bands around a central sun, halo-lit on a cream gallery wall above a pale oak bench.
excerpt: When ancestral art moves beyond decoration, it ceases to sit passively on a wall; it becomes the architectural skin of the room, shaping light, sound, and emotional stillness.
